name: Bryen Jordan, PhD
alt: Bryen Jordan, PhD – Principal Investigator, Neuroscientist, neuron-glia signaling and intellectual disability
bio: Bryen Jordan performed his postdoctoral work at NYU Langone School of Medicine in the lab of HHMI member Dr. Edward Ziff, where he characterized the proteomic composition of synapses and elucidated a novel synapse-to-nucleus signaling pathway. Bryen obtained his PhD in Pharmacology from NYU School of Medicine, under the mentorship of Lakshmi Devi, studying Opioid receptor dimerization and its effects on pharmacology. Prior to this, Bryen obtained his undergraduate degree in Chemical Engineering at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute

name: Ana Cicvaric, PhD
interest: Myelin pathology as a causal mechanism in NDD; pro-myelinating therapies.
bio: My research focuses on how disruptions in myelination contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly autism spectrum disorders (ASD). Building on evidence that myelin dynamically regulates neural circuit function, we hypothesize that deficits in oligodendrocyte development and myelin formation are key drivers of ASD-related phenotypes rather than secondary consequences. Using high-confidence ASD mouse models, we link cellular mechanisms to behavioral outcomes by investigating how loss of ASD-associated proteins impacts oligodendrocyte development, myelin structure, neural signaling, and behavior. In parallel, we test whether pharmacological strategies that promote myelination, such as clemastine, can restore myelin integrity and rescue disease-relevant phenotypes. By connecting glial biology to circuit dysfunction, this work aims to uncover fundamental disease mechanisms and identify new therapeutic opportunities

name: Dylann Cordova-Martinez, MS
alt: Dylann Cordova-Martinez, MS – PhD Candidate studying SCN8A function in oligodendrocytes and myelination
interest: SCN8A function in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
bio: Graduate research on the role of SCN8A/Nav1.6 in oligodendrocyte physiology and its impact on myelin dynamics and circuit function.

name: Saunil "Sonu" Dobariya
alt: Saunil “Sonu” Dobariya – PhD Candidate investigating neuron-OPC synapses
bio: Synapses are a specialized form of communication previously thought to be unique to neuronal cells. When a neuron forms synapses with a non-neuronal cell, what does that mean how does it differ from a typical neuronal synapse? Neurons form glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses with the glial cell known as oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), but little is known of the synaptic properties of these non-canonical synapses and even less is known about their protein composition in mammalian models. My work focuses on characterizing these synapses at the proteomic and electrophysiological level in rodent primary cultures and tissue, assessing changes in neuron-OPC synaptic function and OPC maturation upon specific knockdown or deletion of known postsynaptic proteins in OPCs, such as AIDA-1

name: Jenny Diaz-Rodriguez
alt: Jenny Diaz-Rodriguez – PhD Candidate studying neurotransmitter release by oligodendrocyte lineage cells
bio: Oligodendrocyte lineage cells (OLCs), including oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and mature oligodendrocytes, are well known for their role in myelination. However, recent findings suggest that they also release neurotransmitters such as GABA, and that their ablation leads to reduced neuronal excitatory activity. My research focuses on elucidating how neurotransmitter release by OLCs influences oligodendrocyte maturation, myelination, and neuronal activity.
